data.content_ref: inline:The target's 'least-worst' comparative criterion is internally incoherent when applied to untested rivals. The mechanism states that preferring T means 'recognizing that T has already withstood attempts to destroy it, whereas rivals may not have.' But a purely historical record cannot distinguish between (a) a theory that survived severe tests and (b) a theory that was never tested at all: both have zero failures on their record. If the account is strictly non-inductive and confined to past facts, then an untested theory U has an equally 'clean' historical record as a well-tested theory T — neither has been destroyed. The 'least-worst' judgment therefore cannot rationally prefer T over U without importing the assumption that the severity of past testing carries epistemic weight beyond mere survival, which is itself an inductive bridge between test-severity and reliability. The target's own countercondition acknowledges that 'resilience in the past is logically irrelevant to resilience in the future without an inductive bridge,' but the target fails to recognize that even the comparative past-ranking ('T has withstood more than U') presupposes that withstanding tests is more significant than merely not being tested — a significance claim that is not derivable from the bare historical record alone. Thus the heuristic cannot even get off the ground as a purely historical comparison.
